clinicalPearls: SCA27 involves the FGF14 gene, encoding fibroblast growth factor 14, an intracellular protein that regulates neuronal ion channels and excitability, and two distinct mechanisms are now recognised
The point-mutation form (SCA27A) tends to present earlier, in childhood or young adulthood, with tremor, cerebellar signs and cognitive, behavioural or psychiatric features
The recently described repeat-expansion form (SCA27B), caused by an intronic GAA expansion, has emerged as one of the commonest causes of late-onset hereditary ataxia
SCA27B typically presents in older adults, frequently with episodic symptoms at onset, downbeat nystagmus and slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia
Some patients with SCA27B respond symptomatically to acetazolamide or an aminopyridine, which is a useful therapeutic and diagnostic clue
Diagnosis of SCA27B requires targeted sizing of the FGF14 GAA repeat by repeat-primed PCR or long-read methods, as standard panels and exome miss it, whereas SCA27A needs sequencing
Brain MRI commonly shows cerebellar atrophy, though it may be mild or unremarkable early on
FGF14 testing should now be considered in unexplained late-onset or episodic ataxia, particularly with downbeat nystagmus
reference.pathophysiology: SCA27 is caused by disruption of FGF14, which encodes an intracellular fibroblast growth factor that binds voltage-gated sodium channels at the axon initial segment and tunes neuronal firing, especially in Purkinje cells. Loss-of-function point mutations (SCA27A) reduce FGF14 activity, while the intronic GAA repeat expansion (SCA27B) is thought to impair transcription and lower FGF14 expression; both diminish channel regulation. The resulting Purkinje cell dysfunction and degeneration produce cerebellar ataxia and downbeat nystagmus, with the point-mutation form additionally causing tremor and neuropsychiatric features.
additionalDifferentials: Episodic ataxia type 2 (CACNA1A), which also causes downbeat nystagmus and responds to acetazolamide
Other late-onset sporadic or hereditary cerebellar ataxias
RFC1-related CANVAS and late-onset ataxia with neuropathy
Structural causes of downbeat nystagmus at the craniocervical junction
additionalInvestigations: Targeted sizing of the FGF14 GAA repeat by repeat-primed PCR or long-read sequencing for SCA27B
FGF14 sequencing to detect point mutations in suspected SCA27A
Brain MRI to assess cerebellar atrophy and exclude craniocervical structural lesions
Testing for CACNA1A (episodic ataxia type 2) and RFC1 (CANVAS) where features overlap
Screening for acquired ataxia (thyroid function, vitamins B12 and E, coeliac serology)
A monitored therapeutic trial of acetazolamide where episodic symptoms are prominent
redFlags: Rapid progression or an atypical course suggesting an acquired or paraneoplastic cause
A structural lesion at the craniocervical junction as an alternative cause of downbeat nystagmus
Prominent autonomic failure pointing to multiple system atrophy
Dysphagia with aspiration risk requiring swallow assessment
reference.prognosis: SCA27B is generally slowly progressive and many patients remain ambulant for years, with a proportion gaining symptomatic benefit from acetazolamide; SCA27A has a more variable course with earlier onset and additional tremor and neuropsychiatric features, but overall life expectancy is often relatively preserved.
pitfalls: Missing the GAA expansion because standard gene panels and exome do not detect it
Failing to consider FGF14 in older adults with unexplained or episodic ataxia
Overlooking a therapeutic trial of acetazolamide when episodic features are present
Mislabelling episodic attacks as functional or as isolated vestibular disease
Not counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and the reduced penetrance seen with the repeat expansion
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
